slides.title: Robust Geometric Queries
slides.notes: Open by framing the introduction as the course contract. The book is not only a catalog of formulas; it teaches a way to turn geometry into representations, parameter domains, numerical tests, and residual checks. Emphasize that every later distance, intersection, fitting, and containment routine will reuse this same pattern.

slides.title: A Graphics Query Has A Shape
slides.notes: Use this map to connect the source orientation with the notebook route. A geometry program receives primitives, chooses parameters, searches a feasible domain, and then reports both an answer and evidence that the answer is trustworthy. The important habit is to inspect the domain and the residual, not just the final Boolean or distance.

slides.title: Parameter Domains Unify Many Queries
slides.notes: The chapter's first major idea is that different objects can share the same analytic skeleton. Points, segments, triangles, rectangles, tetrahedra, and boxes differ in dimension and constraints, but closest point queries often minimize one squared-distance function over a bounded parameter set. That viewpoint explains why a single method can transfer across many primitives.

slides.title: Floating Point Is A Model, Not The Reals
slides.notes: Pause on the notation because it separates mathematical intent from machine representation. The real number r is not stored directly; the implementation stores a nearby floating point value. Once arithmetic also rounds, familiar identities such as associativity can fail, so tests must be written for the machine model rather than for ideal real arithmetic.

slides.title: Cancellation And The Quadratic Example
slides.notes: This slide turns the classic quadratic formula warning into a graphics habit. When two nearly equal large quantities are subtracted, significant digits disappear. The stable form chooses the root formula according to the sign of b and then checks the polynomial residual, which is exactly the notebook's final sanity check.

slides.title: Boolean Logic Needs Tolerance Bands
slides.notes: Use the diagonal split as a small version of mesh point location. In exact arithmetic, a point near the shared edge belongs to one triangle or the edge case. In floating point, two triangle tests can both reject it unless the implementation records a tolerance band and reports the near-boundary state explicitly.

slides.title: Degenerate Inputs Are Ordinary Inputs
slides.notes: This is the high-level warning slide. Collinear, coplanar, cocircular, tangent, and almost singular cases are not rare exceptions in graphics pipelines; they occur through modeling, animation, imported data, and finite precision. The implementation plan should name the degeneracy and choose a policy before the downstream routine depends on the answer.

slides.title: Tangency Changes The Numerical Problem
slides.notes: Explain that root finding is geometric, not only algebraic. A transverse intersection usually produces a sign change, so bracketing methods can see it. Tangential first contact has even multiplicity, so the sign may not change at all. Collision detection must therefore look for contact structure, not only sign reversal.

slides.title: Symmetry Is A Debugging Invariant
slides.notes: Order dependence is a practical test for algorithm design. If a segment intersection predicate changes when the two input segments are swapped, either the mathematical cases were split asymmetrically or floating point tolerances were applied inconsistently. Treat this as a unit test because later algorithms silently assume such predicates are stable.

slides.title: Chapter Contract For The Course
slides.notes: Close by making the contract operational. For each later chapter, students should ask what representation is used, which parameter domain is searched, what invariant is preserved, what residual is checked, and which failure mode must be surfaced. This gives the whole course a consistent debugging vocabulary.
